nodes.label: Device A (Nucleus)
nodes.summary: Sync engine in Rust. Keeps Remote, Local and Synced trees and a planner that outputs operations to converge them.
nodes.details: Deterministic Control thread, fuzzed with seeded randomized simulation (CanopyCheck for the planner, Trinity for concurrency). Moves are atomic and shared items have globally unique IDs.

nodes.label: Device B (Nucleus)
nodes.summary: Another client of the same account, running the same engine.

nodes.label: Metadata servers
nodes.summary: Commit a file's blocklist and answer "need blocks" for the ones the store lacks. Backed by Edgestore.
nodes.details: The post describes the commit call returning "need blocks". The server component's name and layout beyond that are not given.

nodes.label: Edgestore (metadata)
nodes.summary: Sharded-MySQL metadata store with Entities and Associations, stateless Cores routing to shard masters, a replicated cache layer, strong consistency by default.
nodes.details: As of that post: several trillion entries, millions of queries per second, 5–9s availability. Older figures.

nodes.label: Block servers
nodes.summary: Accept uploaded blocks directly from clients. Streaming sync lets a downloader prefetch blocks of an uncommitted file from server memory.
nodes.details: Blocks are up to 4 MB, SHA-256 hashed. The downloader aims to stay "just one blockserver network call behind the uploading client".

nodes.label: Block Index
nodes.summary: Maps block hash to cell, bucket and checksum. A giant sharded MySQL cluster behind an RPC layer.

nodes.label: Magic Pocket cells
nodes.summary: Self-contained clusters of about 50 PB raw. Blocks live in 1 GB buckets on volumes of storage nodes, replicated first and then erasure coded.
nodes.details: The erasure-coding scheme and parameters are not given in the posts. Blocks are immutable. Repair starts when a node is offline for 15 minutes.

nodes.label: Second zone
nodes.summary: Every block is stored in at least two zones, and is written to the remote zone within about a second of the local upload.
nodes.details: Zones: western, central and eastern US (as of the post).

nodes.label: Change notification
nodes.summary: How device B learns that something changed (push or long-poll). The standard design. The mechanism is not described in the posts we read.
nodes.details: Treat as a design placeholder, not a statement about Dropbox's implementation.

nodes.label: Magic Pocket (block store)
nodes.summary: Dropbox's in-house immutable block store: Block Index, cells of buckets and volumes, and a second zone.
nodes.details: Grouping container: it names the units the sources describe together. The components inside it are listed in the Components view.

nodes.label: Dropbox user
nodes.summary: Edits files on one or more devices.

flows.name: Edit a file on device A

steps.caption: Nucleus hashes the file into 4 MB SHA-256 blocks and tries to commit the blocklist.
The server replies "need blocks" listing only the blocks it does not already have.
The client uploads just those blocks straight to a block server, not through the metadata path.
Blocks are stored in Magic Pocket: immutable, hash-keyed and aggregated into buckets.
The Block Index records where each hash lives (cell, bucket, checksum).
Each block is copied to a second zone within about a second.
The client commits the blocklist again. This time nothing is missing.
The file's metadata now points at the new blocklist in Edgestore.

flows.name: See the change on device B

steps.caption: After the commit, the change is announced. The mechanism is a standard design, not a documented Dropbox detail.
Device B wakes up and updates its Remote Tree.
B asks the metadata servers for the new state. Its planner diffs Remote, Local and Synced trees to decide what to download.
B fetches only the blocks it lacks. With streaming sync it can start before the uploader's final commit.
